utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Case Number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Stefan Waespi, Daryl Mundis, assisted by Mr. Andres Vatter, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the appearances for the other Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon assisted by Mr. Nermin Mulalic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber bids good morning to all those people present on the 1st of February and the 174th sitting that we are holding. Before bringing in the witness the Chamber, which was yesterday addressed by the question of hearsay testimony, wishes to say the following. But we're going to give under arrest ruling in private session, as the matter was raised in private session yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session. The witness that started testifying yesterday will be brought into the courtroom in order to answer questions put to him by the Prosecution in the course of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel. If you hear me, can you say so. You have been brought in with some delay, but we had some procedural matters to deal with that's why you were brought into the courtroom at 20 to 10.00. Without further delay, I'm going to give the floor to the Prosecution to continue their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Waespi: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have about an hour and 25 minutes left according to calculations, and I want to spend the first part on issues unrelated to the Mujahedin. You talked yesterday about the Kacuni checkpoint incident of 25th of January, I believe. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did mention, though, that two Croats were killed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mention that two Croats were killed, no I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me just remind you of what you testified in Kordic, and you also discussed it in your book on page 231. In Kordic, transcript pages 12.371 you were asked by -- I believe it was the Defence, Mr. Sawyers of Mr. Kordic at the time. And his question was, and I quote him: "In connection with the fighting that occurred, sir, there is no question that the spark that set off the fighting was the murder of two Croats at the Kacuni checkpoint. And you subsequently had conversations with General Hadzihasanovic and Colonel Merdan about that. Correct?" Your answer: "Yes." "Q. In fact, you told both General Hadzihasanovic and Colonel Merdan one day later that they were at least responsible for the outbreak of the fighting that occurred on the 25th of January, and they both agreed, did they not?" Your answer: "Yes, I think I certainly told them. Whether they necessarily agreed, I can't remember." Do you remember having testified according to these lines?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me go on to the -- another aspect of those days, and it's about Dusina. Again in Kordic you were asked, again on 17th January, 1999, this time by Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, it's pages 12.374. "Q. All right. Did you receive any information from your soldiers or other sources of information that you had at your disposal regarding massacres of Croat civilians at the villages of Dusina and Lasva, sir?" Your answer: "I think I did and I think I've referred to them already, that sort of evidence."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Yes." Your answer: "Most certainly I tried very hard to investigate any reports of Croats being massacred by Muslims."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Just one question on that regard. Did you ever hear about anyone being prosecuted or administratively punished, removed from command or anything like that in connection with those massacres at Dusina and Lasva on January the 25th and 26th, 1993, sir?" And you answer: "I think that Merdan told me that the people concerned were going to be court-martialed. "Q. And do you know whether they ever were? "A. No." Do you remember testifying under oath like that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've reminded me. But, yes, I think that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's go onto a point about the Geneva Conventions. You told us, I believe, that the soldiers on the ground not necessarily knew what the Geneva Conventions meant -- or at least what that is, the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you would agree with me that they certainly knew -- every soldier knows that it's a crime, it's illegal under any system to massacre civilians, unarmed civilians, to execute captured prisoners who lay down their weapons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [In English] Stop. [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. If my learned friend wishes to quote the Geneva Conventions, I must say that the word "massacre" is not part of the Geneva Conventions. If he wants to mention a crime, he may quote any convention but he cannot use big words to reinforce his quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence is saying that you may quote the Geneva Conventions, but that according to the Defence the word "massacre" is not a word that is part of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness said that the people on the ground didn't know the Geneva Conventions. The articles -- I don't know the Geneva Conventions in every article, so my point is: I want to know what the witness knows, what the state of knowledge was on the ground in regard to whether somebody is allowed to execute prisoners. I would like to know whether the witness has any knowledge about that, because he said the people on the ground didn't know the letter of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. So you want, Witness, to be precise and say what the people on the ground knew about the Geneva Conventions and how they interpreted the Geneva Conventions. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question is: Would every soldier in your knowledge, and you had contact with all these people, you were in the scene almost half a year, perhaps even more. Do these soldiers know that it's not allowed to massacre civilians?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: My belief is that every human being knows that massacring anyone is a crime. My belief is also that everyone should know that shooting prisoners is not acceptable. Now, when I say the "Geneva Conventions," I specifically mean the treatment of prisoners and how you deal with people. And I am not an expert on the Geneva Conventions, I just know the basic outlines of how to deal with people. But I would always emphasise the basic points that came from law, whether they were Geneva Conventions or not. You do not kill people, civilians particularly, and you treat prisoners properly, with respect. And those are the kind of things I would say all the time. Some of the soldiers on the ground, specifically in places right on the front line, I would necessarily -- I would re-emphasise this point when I was visiting, that if they did take prisoners, they were not to hurt them once they got them under power. I didn't talk to them and say, Do you know about the Geneva Conventions? I would say, You are not allowed to do this under law, because the Geneva Conventions would mean so little to so many people. But the commanders - let's be clear - the commanders on all sides were professional military officers like I was, and they understood the Geneva Conventions. But it's quite difficult when you suddenly have an army come from nothing, for them to understand all the details of how you treat prisoners. After all, the British army is not without sin itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. And when you talk about commanders, that would General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, General Hadzihasanovic was a professional officer like I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me touch upon another issue which you mentioned almost Beaussou yesterday. You told us about the death of your driver and that you believed that a BH soldier was responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my belief. I have no proof.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you then went on to say that, and I quote you -- you also had incidents with the HVO. "I don't believe that they were under instructions from their chain of command to engage the United Nations. In fact, I'm pretty sure they weren't, and that includes the HVO. So I used to put it down to lack of control, out of control soldiers, such as on the 13th of January." Do you remember having said that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thankfully I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave I would like to show the witness a document, and I informed counsel yesterday orally, I faxed it to them. It's a two-page -- in fact, one-page order by General Blaskic which is very telling and which appears to contradict at least what the witness says. Perhaps it refreshes his memory because he was on the ground. Now, stated -- it's an order classified "urgent, urgent, urgent," to all -- to various units by General Blaskic, Colonel at that time, dated 18th April, 1993, at 0800 hours in the morning. And if I just can read out the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would kindly ask my learned friend to clarify -- I see what the witness has said. He said that the two armies did not have any express orders to attack the United Nations. I don't see the purpose of this document. The witness says that neither the BiH army nor the HVO ever received an order to attack the UN forces. And I don't see how this document can be helpful with that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this some sort of confusion that we are facing here? The Defence says that the witness never said that the party in conflict ever had an order to attack UN vehicles. Are we talking at cross-purposes here? Mr. Prosecutor, what are you trying to achieve with your questions here?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The witness said he believed that several units were out of control, and he gave an example that he -- his driver was attacked by a BiH driver. He gave another example without foundation that the HVO would also shoot at UN, but he said that wasn't commanded, it wasn't controlled. And here we have a clear example of Colonel Blaskic ordering that UN troops be shot at. And there will be another document saying that ten days later in fact we know they were shot at. And that is a contradiction of what the witness said, and perhaps he can help us whether that changes his opinion that indeed in particular HVO troops shot at UN and were indeed commanded and ordered to do so, not just out of control elements as the witness had told us yesterday. And since he was on the ground, I think it's probably interesting for him to see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you surprised to see this order?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am surprised a little, but looking at the date of the order, if you note the date it's round about the time of the Lasva valley activities, and my soldiers were indeed restricted in their movements at this time as I recall. I said, if I can remember correctly what I said just earlier, that out of control soldiers, not elements -- I mean, individuals might have opened fire. I felt quite strongly that actually there weren't orders given out by people like Colonel Blaskic to attack me. Indeed on several occasions - at least one occasion I can remember, so I'll be precise - at least one occasion I went to Blaskic after I'd personally been engaged quite heavily by snipers and RPG-7s fired at me personally. And my complaint to Blaskic was: Your soldiers opened fire at me this morning, personally at me, and I should have killed them or I could have killed them in response. In fact, I aimed off when I responded by firing myself. And his answer to me was: You should have killed them because I have given orders that they are not to attack you. Now, I took "you" as being the United Nations, not me personally. It may well have been me personally, but I took it as the United Nations forces. And it's on that sort of principle that I say I didn't believe that the HVO or the ABiH had direct orders to attack my soldiers; however, this document here dated the 18th of April suggests that soldiers of the HVO might actually in the pursuit of stopping us going into the so-called operational area might open fire at us. So I've never seen this document before. I accept that I might be wrong. I've said that it's my opinion, not a fact. And I accept that at that time it was extremely difficult, because my orders to my soldiers were quite simple: Get into the middle of the battle, take our vehicles straight in the middle there, make sure they are clearly visible with their white sides and the United Nations on it, do not open fire unless someone opens fire at you, but if they open fire at you, kill them. I wanted to try and stop the fighting, and I also gave instructions for anyone that was hurt, whether they be ABiH, HVO, or civilians, regardless of their status, they were to be picked up and dealt with properly in accordance with civilised behaviour and brought into hospitals and, if necessary, our hospital direct. Those are the instructions I gave. Now, I'm sorry if I'm slightly at variance with this document, but I've never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you agree with me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the record, I would like to clarify as following. Colonel, when you were shot at, was it before the 18th of April or after the 18th of April? It would be of some importance to know that. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would look through my diary, Your Honour, to find it. The incident was I think at -- I definitely -- I would need time just to look because it would be in my diary because there were two pigs that were dead there as well. And that would -- I seem to remember writing something about pigs and the smell, but I don't know -- right now I can't give you an honest answer -- I can't give you the right answer, whether it was before. I think it was probably -- most probably afterwards, and I think I had also General Morillion around on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that this order shows actions on the ground were probably were probably coordinated than they appeared to you at first sight?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forgive me, sir, I never said that the HVO didn't have coordinated actions on the ground. This was a deliberate attack in -- a deliberate and pre-planned attack that started on the morning of the 16th. If I implied that or said that, I'm sorry, I've made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've said that before, and there's evidence on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's Exhibit DH205, an ECMM document dated 28th April, 1993, signed by Mr. Thebault that on page 2 of this document -- and perhaps that could be distributed as well again. The reference I'm interested in is on page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next paragraph after the middle it says: "Between Kiseljak and Zenica we are unable to see many burning places. We were able to see many burning place in HVO-controlled area, in particular Gomionica, 3 kilometres northwest of Kiseljak, where access was yesterday denied by HVO to ECMM combat joint patrol which after a new attempt today was fired at." That appears to be a direct consequence perhaps of Mr. Blaskic's order, and you remember in paragraph 5 of this order it said: "Any arbitrary behaviour will be severely punished." Do you remember that incident raised by Mr. Thebault where CanBat was shot at?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't because it was outside the area -- the Canadian Battalion was dealing with ECMM up towards Kiseljak. Although I often patrolled up there, I do not remember this particular incident, except I was shot at around that position on a couple of occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Next, Colonel, let's go on to -- briefly to the milinfosums. Again, would you agree with me that informing your superiors was one of your foremost duties?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these milinfosums were part of that duty?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I believe you submitted a milinfosum one every day over time you were in the area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever hear back from BH command in Kiseljak, Mr. Morillion, or perhaps MOD in London, if they received, any complaints about not properly assessed materials in these milinfosums?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I did, otherwise I would have paid more attention to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who exactly drafted the daily milinfosums?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: A mixture of people, the operations officer, perhaps my second in command, perhaps the intelligence cell perhaps the duty watchkeeper, normally a young officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can one tell from looking at the face of a milinfosum on a given day who the drafter might have been?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that would be difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it recorded in a war diary who the drafter or perhaps the duty officer on a specific day was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe not -- you see, probably not the duty officer -- the answer is probably not. We didn't have time -- forgive me. We did not have time to do everything written down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'll come to milinfosum in a second. I also want to clarify something you mentioned in relation to Mr. Hadzihasanovic yesterday. I asked you whether you knew there might be incidents in these milinfosums that would reflect that Mr. Hadzihasanovic wasn't speaking the truth or was less accurate. And your answer was: "It's quite possible," but you weren't able to give a concrete example of such a behaviour?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. And I was not able to give a concrete example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you something about milinfosum, but first: Who would usually meet with Hadzihasanovic, General Hadzihasanovic, the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably me. Probably me, and possibly my second in command, and possibly the company commander, that sort of level. After all, General Hadzihasanovic was the top officer of the BiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have an interpreter with you when you talked to him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I can't see how I could have communicated with General Hadzihasanovic without an interpreter. I can't absolutely say that when I was on my own perhaps at an ECMM meeting, and I just happened to meet him, that I had an interpreter right by my side. But for any kind of formal meeting, I couldn't go to see General Hadzihasanovic without an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you always use the same interpreter?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had two, three military interpreters, two captains and one sergeant, and I hired 16 local interpreters trying to balance in a kind of way between ethnic Serb, Croat, Muslim in that number, but it wasn't easy. But the very best interpreter I had was a lady called Dobrila Kolaba who was a Bosnian Serb who was very sadly shot just after the end of my tour. But it might have been the kind of person, the kind of interpreter I might have taken to see General Hadzihasanovic would be either a military interpreter or someone like Dobrila Kolaba, who I trusted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever use (redacted) as a interpreter?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Many times?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you start using him, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nick Stansfield was the first interpreter, military interpreter I had. And (redacted) arrived a little bit later. I can't remember exactly when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it in 1993 or already in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that be reflected in your notes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not necessarily. The interpreter didn't -- forgive me, didn't really matter. I just wanted to be -- my words to be as properly presented as possible. However, I would take normally a military interpreter into a difficult -- a very difficult situation to safeguard the civilian interpreter from, perhaps, reprisals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is the CO 1? That's a reference in a milinfosum who went to see General Hadzihasanovic. Who would that be?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: CO 1?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps if the witness could be shown an already existing exhibit. Mr. President, it's at tab 2 in the binder P370.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could look at the first paragraph A it talks about a CO 1 PWO met with Enver Hadzihasanovic who initially spoke about renewed fighting in Mostar of the cease-fire between Halilovic and Petkovic. He mentioned involvement by regular HVO brigades against -- in the fighting, specifically mentioning 113 and 114 Brigades from Split and elements of 114 Brigade. During conversation, Hadzihasanovic threatened action against Vitez and Busovaca. When questioned about the deployment of 314 Brigade in the area of Preocica, he flatly denied that it was stating they were on the front line against the Chetniks. Comment. This directly contradicts a non-fact. Comment ends.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could answer this without -- this is very easy for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My learned friend put a question to the witness, and that is: What does CO 1 mean? And to specify he showed him a document to illustrate what this abbreviation means. I am surprised that my colleague is not familiar with this abbreviation at this stage of the proceedings, but the problem is that the witness has not been given a chance to answer, to say, what it means. And also, no reason, no grounds, have been established for showing him this document which was drafted after he left Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. When you put this question, I noted that the date of the document is the 15th of May, 1993, and if he left before then we may have a problem. Perhaps it would be best for him to tell us what CO 1 stands for.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just quickly respond to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: PWO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we are not testifying, unlike, perhaps, what sometimes I see from the Defence bench, so it's not up to me to say what the CO 1 is in the abbreviation. So it's up to the witness to do that, and I wanted to give him a chance. In looking at the exact wording of the CO 1 -- and if he left two days earlier, this may be a follow-up of what was discussed in an earlier conversation. And his successor, if CO 1 indeed means his successor, then he may have raised something he was briefed about. So this witness certainly is able to give a comment about the meeting with Hadzihasanovic, and he was in fact willing to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we hear your comment, Colonel, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours and sir, the CO 1 confused me. CO 1 PWO does not. Commanding officer of the 1st Battalion, the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment of Yorkshire, which I totally understand is extremely confusing if you haven't been brought up with British army abbreviations. And it is true, this is dated after I had left Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us about -- something about this deployment of -- or this threat by Hadzihasanovic. When it says "again," was that something you had experienced before?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I was never in the slightest bit threatened by General Hadzihasanovic. The only indication not of threat was that he was fighting to preserve his area; it wasn't a threat -- I never had a threat made against the United Nations by General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Here in fact he doesn't talk about United Nations or yourself; he talks about Vitez.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. He's probably in that case talking generically about the HVO who were in control of Vitez. I wasn't in control of Vitez. My camp was on the outskirts and I wasn't meant to be in control of anything. I was meant to be escorting humanitarian aid, which I accept caused me huge problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it you can't comment on the comment here: "A direct contradiction of a known fact"? You don't know what these facts which are contradicted?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. If we could move on to a new subject, and that's the killing of two British soldiers or mercenaries. I believe you told us that there were Danes and Germans in the area. And in your book you mention the killing of two British soldiers. And I would like to briefly paraphrase and I don't know --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I stop you there. They weren't British soldiers; they were mercenaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I just wanted to ask you about them. Their names were Ted Skinner and Derek Arlo McBride?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know if you want to have the book open, I just want to read a couple of passages on these gentleman. You said that you first met them outside the hospital in Travnik when you went to see the doctor there, and that's on page 93 of your book. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they apparently worked with the Muslim army; that's what you were told?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what they said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And specifically you talk about Ted, Ted Skinner, who explained to you that he was: "A captain in the Muslim army and that his job was training and medical evacuation."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, can I explain that before that, perhaps not in the book, his approach to me that he came to me and saluted me and told me - maybe it wasn't the book, I can't remember - he told me that he knew I disliked mercenaries and I didn't want to have anything to do with mercenaries and I had told mercenaries collectively to get out of my area. Even so he approached me and apologised and then told me this, which softened me a little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in fact later you became interested in the fate and indeed usefulness of mercenaries as a source of information. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if people come to me and give me information, that's great, but it didn't change my basic view of mercenaries, that they had no right to be in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but it's correct that previously you had decided not to get connected to them. But later you started to use them as a considerable source of information?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. If they brought information to us, we would listen. We did not seek out, to the best of my knowledge none of my intelligence officers went out and deliberately cultivated mercenaries as sources of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to put words in your mouth. Let me just read out what the book says and perhaps I mis-paraphrased it. Quote from page 92: "Although in principle I had previously decided not to have anything to do with mercenaries, as I wanted very much to disassociate our activities from theirs, it was not easy in practice. Actually they could be a considerable source of information. And so I began to talk to some of them."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't seek them out. They -- if I came across them I would repeat my message, which was: Get out. And indeed with McBride and Skinner, I repeated that when I saw them because I thought they were very vulnerable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you called them a considerable source of information.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because they told us what was going on on the front lines, boasting maybe, but they told us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go on about what these two gentlemen told you. They told you: "They lived in the Muslim barracks at Travnik and received hardly any pay, calling themselves helpers rather than mercenaries, they claimed that they were in Bosnia because it was such a tragic situation. 'The Muslims needed all the help they could get,' they said."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now unfortunately they were killed and the Trial Chamber has heard evidence about that before. And I quote again from your book, it's now on page 247: "As Ted and Derrick" - the two mercenaries - "had worked for the Bosnian Muslims, their bodies were taken to the city morgue in Zenica. I spoke to General Merdan about the matter. He knew both men well and was very unhappy about what had happened. He also assured me that they had not been killed because they were British or because people thought they were connected to us." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember writing it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me perhaps conclude before the break -- yes, my colleague just mentions a request for clarification. What do you mean by "Muslim barracks in Travnik"? Can you be more specific.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a building where people -- soldiers would stay. It wasn't a -- I mean, I think it -- I couldn't quite work out what it was, but there was a place where the ABiH would customarily have a headquarters and some sleeping accommodation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to briefly quote and I'm coming to a command and control aspect, what you said in the Blaskic trial, and it's on page 23.847, 18th June, 1999. Just one sentence: "I put it simply. A commander is responsible for the action of his soldiers. There is a difference between responsibility and the actual crime itself, but overall responsibility rests with that commander."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my belief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, if you were told that your troops had committed crimes in an area, you would do all you could to try to investigate that crime?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually I'd do more than that; I'd call in the special investigation branch because I would not want people to think that I had in any way tried to hush it up. But that is in an army that's got an established organisation. But you're right, if my troops commit a crime and it was my constant demand to all sides if the commanders knew about a crime or were told about a crime in their operational area of responsibility, they had a duty to investigate and identify what had happened and to punish if necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one of the first persons or person to talk to would be the commander, the local commander, of that unit in that area, company commander, battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: You -- in the circumstances of Central Bosnia at the time, yes, it would be likely that I would go directly to the top man and someone else would go to the local area, or I would do both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about your unit. When one of your subordinate commanders in his area of responsibility, his unit perhaps had done something, then you would certainly almost as a first reaction to talk to him and ask him, not necessarily as a suspect, ask him: Explain me what's happened?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Tell me what's happened, and why hadn't I known about it before?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me move on now, Mr. President, to the issue of Mujahedin. And I believe we have a few minutes left, although we can also stop for the break and I can start this last subject after the break. I am in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it's better to have the break now. It is 10.25. We'll have our regular break, and we'll resume work at around 10 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are resuming after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could go into private session just for the beginning of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar, can we please go into private session?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me continue with the information you told us, you know, about this source. We also had a person testifying in this Tribunal who met with a Mujahedin, and I would like to -- and this was a British journalist. Perhaps you might even though him. His name is Andrew Hogg and he worked at that time for the --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sunday Times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Sunday times. Yes. And I believe he even came to the area again a second time, in April 1993, he went to Milici. Do you remember having seen him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember his name, I remember his face; I don't know when I saw him frequently at the start and perhaps in April 1993 -- in fact, I do see to remember that I saw him in April 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very early August 1992 he met with Mujahedin and he provided the Trial Chamber with a tape, and a transcript was made. And that appears to contradict what, you know, the information you provided us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So, Mr. President, I would like to show the witness tab 7, and this is Prosecution Exhibit 112, tab 2, of 112.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see a transcript of conversation between Andrew Hogg, journalist, and Abdul Aziz?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I just want to refer you to one transcript that's on page 2, and I want to quote what Aziz who apparently spoke English very well. "There is no specific area we are fighting, but different area. One thing I want to tell you about my Mujahedin is that we are under guidance or you can say control of Muslim forces. My Mujahedin and my rules or whatever your condition is, that we are not leader here. We don't like to have our own first line or our own base. We working under their guidance and their control." And let me also tell you that for Mr. Hogg to interview this person, he had to go through the ABiH. And in fact, this gentleman, Mr. Abdul Aziz told him, and I quote --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Maybe my learned friend could give us the date of this interview and then we could see where the witness was at that time; and which is even more important, he seems to be saying that the BiH army was involved. He has to give us his source. That would help us understand how could BiH army be involved in such an incident if it didn't exist at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please be more specific with regard to the date when this interview was conducted between the journalist and Mr. Abdul Aziz? We have to bear in mind that they -- the Defence finds it important that at the time the BiH army did not exist, so can you give us the date of this interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it's already on the record. I said he met with him in August of 1992. It just disappeared from the screen right now. So that's the time this person talked to him, and again this is cross-examination. I have a statement of a source who -- which appears to contradict what the witness told us earlier, and I can certainly ask him -- and he even knows the journalist, you know, whether that changes his view about whether the Mujahedin were indeed part of the 3rd Corps or not. Perhaps he considers then his information to be unreliable. I would just like to ask him and in fact continue my question that the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Mujahedin who was the interviewee, the partner, to Mr. Hogg told Mr. Hogg, and I quote: "If you want an interview, come back here with permission from the Bosnian army. I will grant an interview if they allow it." So if you hear this -- you know, the circumstances how this interview was conducted and indeed the contents of it, does that surprise you that you hear an obvious connection between the BH army and the Mujahedin in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: It surprises me, and I don't know what to believe about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me move on to another exhibit, and this is tab 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, in my bundle and this is Exhibit 461. I believe Mr. Dixon has something. Perhaps if the witness could not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... exhibit for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Only a brief point. In accordance with Your Honour's decision yesterday that documents can be shown to the witness even if they are documents which he might not have seen at the time or been party to. We have another document here which is an internal document of the 7th Brigade. And I wish to request that in line with the decision Your Honours gave yesterday, that the witness should be asked, if he is going to be shown this document, at the outset of whether or not he recognises this document. In our submission, it does not assist Your Honours at all just to read out the title of the document or who it's signed by; anyone in the courtroom can do that. The important question is whether he recognises anything in this document. In our submission, this is important in respect to the weight that is to be given to these documents. As Your Honours will know, many of these documents were contested documents and then admitted into evidence, but Your Honours made it clear that the weight to be assigned to them would be assigned at a later point once all the evidence had been heard depending on which witnesses could comment on the document and interpret it. And in our submission, if the witness does not recognise this document at all, then it cannot assist Your Honours in determining what weight to give to this document at the end of the day. Our request would be that if he is to be shown it, he should be asked whether he recognises the first and then any further questions, if necessary, can be put thereafter. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I may be heard on this point, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is cross-examination. I need to have a good-faith basis for any leading question I can put to this witness, and it certainly is a good-faith basis if there is an exhibit. It could be even not an exhibit, in our case, whether internal or outside, that doesn't really matter. And again the witness testified that he thought from his assessment the Mujahedin were not connected to the ABiH. This document contradicted it, and I would like to have his comment on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we can have a look at it, if you may. It's Exhibit P461, and I'm just asking whether perhaps you heard about these incidents. This document is -- originates from the 3rd Corps, 7th Muslim -- Mountain Muslim Brigade. It dates 12 April 1993, and it's titled "Report on Members of Our Brigade Taken Prisoner by HVO Members." And it's signed by the assistant commander for morale, religious and legal affairs, Ahmed Hadilovic [phoen]. Let me just read out the -- for the record the first sentence, first paragraph: "Recently there have been an increasing number of cases of HVO members at certain checkpoints unlawfully taking prisoner foreign citizens who are members of the BH army, i.e., volunteers who are in our unit. The command of our brigade asserts that the fact that these prisoners have never participated in fighting against HVO units. More specifically, we have expressly stated to them conscious of the situation that they are only fighting against the Chetniks." And then you can see on the same page some members also of these foreign fighters, where they are from. Now, you would agree with me that this document indeed shows that the -- at least the 7th Muslim Brigade, part of the 3rd Corps, in fact claims that these people are part of the BH army and they want them back?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I've seen this document, but it appears to be a copy of the document underneath, and it appears to be that there are Middle East people, Pakistan, Algeria, who were part of the BiH as volunteers; it appears to show that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you have reason now to start to doubt the veracity of the information you have provided as previously?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this doesn't say this were Mujahedin. I'm looking for a Mujahedin unit here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me go on to the next document, Your Honours, and this is tab number 10 and it's Prosecution Exhibit P541.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is in fact -- and I'm for the first part interested in the second letter, so it's the third page. That's a letter by Mr. Hadzihasanovic dated 2nd April 1993. And it has the heading "Violent Treatment of Foreign Nationals, Volunteers in the BH Army by Members of the HVO." So again Mr. Hadzihasanovic talks about the similar issue, and we don't need to go over it. And he also mentions that some goods of these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My learned friend says that General Hadzihasanovic is involved again. Why again? In the previous document, there is no hint that the document might have originated from the 3rd Corps or General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we all know, again means again. And the Defence has a point saying that General Hadzihasanovic was not mentioned in the previous document, so you can't use the word "again" unless you're saying that the same problem is mentioned here again, in which case we have a different situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And the source of misinformation is my command of the English. I tried in fact to say that again we have an issue, and I confused it with that. So I apologise. I didn't want to say that Mr. Hadzihasanovic was also connected to the earlier document, although I might add that he was the commander of that corps under which -- whose authority the first document originated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's briefly talk about this one. Have you had the chance to glance over the document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've only skimmed it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again here -- I'm sorry, and here the commander of the 3rd Corps shows an interest in these foreign nationals. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we have fortunately - and that's not always occurring in this Tribunal - a response. And this response is from General Blaskic, and you can see it on the first two pages. And it's dated the 3rd April, and he makes reference to Mr. Hadzihasanovic's letter of the 2nd April. And then here I believe we come to an issue raised beforehand about the fourth paragraph. It says: "Four foreign nationals, Mujahedin, were arrested at the Puticevo checkpoint. They had resisted inspection by threatening with their weapons and did not allow the inspection to be carried out." And then it goes on: "All four individuals were arrested and driven to the military prison Busovaca." So he appears to give his assessment to the allegations, and he did request of General Hadzihasanovic. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we see here what's meant -- we can't read the minds of these gentlemen who drafted, but it appears to be one of the subjects is the Mujahedin. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: He says "four foreign nationals (Mujahedin)." You know, one of the problems for all forces in this country was that both the HVO and the BiH were reinforced by people from outside the countries. It is his choice, the word "Mujahedin." It is not mine or yours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. And perhaps just following up from this. What you personally mean when you say "Mujahedin"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I mean a group of people who work as a unit together who come from outside and who are not actually integrated normally into the structure of the army, and may or may not be connected to the army they are supporting. And generally they are more aggressive and fanatical than others. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, and I believe we will come to that when we look at the document. Now, without showing you documents, did you know that a senior member of again the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade requested the 3rd Corps to provide helicopters to transport to the front lines at Igman foreign Mujahedin. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. There is a document describing that. Maybe my learned friend has economised on time and that's why he didn't shown it. However, this document contains an error that has been corrected, but it has not been corrected on the document that was shown to the document [as interpreted]. Can this first be corrected so that the translation is correct, and then the document can be quoted and shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there has been a debate on translation issues arising from that document. The Defence would like to have the witness to be shown a correct translation of the document before he is asked any questions, because the original document did not contain those corrections. Mr. Registrar, can you please find the document, and I believe that from the CLSS we have asked that the right word be communicated to us. To gain time, Mr. Bourgon, can you tell us what the matter was with the translation, what was wrong with the translation? Maybe Mr. Dixon can enlighten us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, I have the document in front of me, it's P616, and the first line of that document was translated incorrectly, and Your Honours confirmed that in the transcript on page 12.173 an onwards. The first line in the incorrect translation said "we have 11 people, Arabs and Turks," but the correct translation which has now been accepted is that "we know," not "have," "we know 11 Arabs and Turks." So if my learned friend is going to put this document to the witness, once again we would request that he's asked whether he recognises the document, but then also the correct version should be put to the witness to see what his comment is, if any. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The debate was whether the document contains the words "we know" or "we have." It's not the same thing obviously. The issue was the difference between "we have" and "we know."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the question perhaps in a way that could solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, were you aware that there was a request for a helicopter flight under -- requested by the 7th Muslim Brigade in order to transport Arabs and Turks to the Igman front line? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is no, but I may have forgotten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [In English] Stop, stop please. [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Maybe my learned friend could give us the date of the document. This would be of assistance to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecution, can you give us the date on the document because this will tell us whether the witness was there at the time. If the document dates from the time when the witness was no longer there, then we have a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. President, it was my mistake; I should have done that. The document dates of 28th August 1993, but my question had been general, whether he had heard of any type of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it your answer remains the same?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it becomes more -- no, I wouldn't have heard of it either. I had no knowledge in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you also aware or not that ABiH identity cards were issued to foreign fighters? Have you heard of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the exhibit I was relying was P626. It's a document from the HVO dating 9th March, 1993, and it's in tab 11 of my bundle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does all of this information, does it change your assessment of whether these Mujahedin were connected to the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not but it's obvious that maybe some foreign nationals were working with the BiH. But it doesn't change my assessment with regard to my definition of the Mujahedin working not under control of the BiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you another document. And before that I would like to ask you whether you have heard in the course of your duties as commander of the 1st Cheshire Battalion, that a normally reliable source has provided information about the Mujahedin and the 7th Muslim Brigade. And I can just quote one piece of that information that perhaps you remember that --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, my learned friend knows very well he's about to quote from a new document. New documents cannot be shown to witnesses unless there's a proper basis established according to your ruling, either that it goes to credibility or it goes to refreshing memory. So this document needs to be considered as a new document. It's one that was only disclosed to us recently, and it mentions a source, although it doesn't say what this source is. And I think this matter does need to be fully debated before it's just slipped in and shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I can briefly respond, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I preceded my question exactly with the foundation, because this is a milinfosum originating from his battalion, and I asked him whether he remembers that a reliable local source provided the information. Apparently it was good enough to be included in this milinfosum, and I think the commander of that battalion ought to know about that. Perhaps he doesn't, because he was busy. I don't doubt that. But I can certainly show it to him; perhaps it refreshes his memory, because he's shown a certain interest in the Mujahedin as developed over time. And I think I'm following the procedure right now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment, Mr. Dixon. I'll give you the floor. The Defence has a document, a milinfosum in which apparently this question is referred to. According to my understanding this is a new document and the Prosecution pursuant to our decision regarding credibility or the refreshment of memory wishes to show this document to the witness. That is the situation as it now stands. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. It is indeed a new document which refers to the 7th Brigade, and our objection would be that this document cannot be shown to the witness to refresh his memory because he's already said in -- perhaps the witness can be asked to leave. I don't want to waste time, but my learned friend is suggesting it, and I agree with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, will you please ask the witness to leave the courtroom for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon, before giving you the floor, we referring to a document which the Chamber is not aware of because it is a new document which was disclosed to you earlier. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Yes, we did receive this document. It's a military information summary. Your Honour, our objection is that the witness has already testified that he knew nothing about the 7th Brigade. And in addition to that, Your Honours, he has stated that he never read or saw any military information summaries. That was not something that he regarded as part of his duties. We, therefore, would object to him being shown the document to seek to refresh his memory when he said quite clearly from his best recollection that he knows nothing about the 7th Brigade. There was no issue in relation to the 7th Brigade and he had taken no view on it. In addition to that he has said that the document that we have in front of us is one that he wouldn't have seen. So in our submission there's no way that his memory can be refreshed from a document which he wouldn't have seen at the time and in relation to matters he said he knew nothing about at the time. He's been asked a question about what he knew about the 7th Brigade and he's answered it. And really what the Prosecution is now seeking to do, in our submission, is introduce a new document in order to strengthen its case. And Your Honour's ruling is quite clear on that. They cannot use new documents to strengthen their case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I give the floor to the Prosecution. If I understand, the Defence's analysis is that the witness has said that he hardly ever heard mention of the 7th Brigade and therefore any questions about the 7th Brigade would be null and void, as he is not in a position to contribute anything regarding the 7th Brigade. However, I don't know the date of this document, but if it is a milinfosum coming from his battalion or his regiment, it would be rather paradoxical that as head of the regiment he was not familiar with that document. So could you tell us the date of that document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. The date is 27 January 1993. That predates the time when it is alleged that Mr. Kubura was the commander of the 7th Brigade as well. But, Your Honour, the witness has said that he never looked at any of these military information summaries, and in our submission, to look at it now can't therefore refresh his memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I may respond, Mr. President. It's not refreshing the memory of whether he has seen the document, it's about refreshing the memory of what was said about the issue of command and control over the Mujahedin. And as he rightly observed, he was the battalion commander and every night this went out to his superiors. And this time -- and it's on tab 6 of your bundle, it's only two pages. And almost 25 per cent is occupied by what this normally reliable source says. And he testified he had these 5.00 meetings, so perhaps that was discussed at this 5.00 meeting and is now reflected in the -- this milinfosum. And you will also note, Your Honours, that this normally reliable source has provided additional information. So it appears to have been a topic beforehand. I really believe that the commander of the battalion must have been appraised of that, and it would surprise me if he hasn't heard of the discussion on the issue of Mujahedin, which was a topic of interest as he told us today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution tells us that this document is dated the 27th of January, 1993. It comes from the witness's regiment, over which the witness had supreme responsibility. This witness and other witnesses have said that every day a milinfosum was drafted, intended for a higher authority. The witness told us that yesterday, in fact. And the Prosecution wishes to ask the witness whether what appears on page 2 of that document, is it not in contradiction with what he might have said up to now. So that is the purpose of the question to be put to the witness. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no objection to the witness being asked about what might have been discussed about the Mujahedin in his daily briefings. He said he was there at a number of those briefings. The issue did arise. My learned friend could ask him about what was discussed, he could put assertions to him about information that might have come up. But in our submission, there is no basis to put this particular document to him and ultimately seek it to be admitted into evidence as a new document. That is the crux of the argument we're making. This is an entirely new document the Prosecution could have introduced during its case; it didn't do so. And in our view, it could only do so in limited circumstances. If the witness has said these are documents he never dealt with, then in our view it shouldn't come into evidence at this point. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we are still not at the stage when the Prosecution is asking to tender the document. So, Mr. Dixon, you are anticipating things. We have still not reached the stage when the Prosecution is asking to tender the document. They have just told us that they are going to refer to a paragraph and ask the witness what he says in response. So, Mr. Usher, will you call the witness back into the courtroom and then we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps if that second page could be put on the ELMO as well, Mr. Usher. It's tab 6. A milinfosum, number 88 of the 27th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have it in your hands?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to start with, on page 1, is that one of your daily milinfo summaries?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which went up the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the UN chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you told us you take full responsibility for it despite the fact that you may never have seen it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you could turn to page number 2 and the second paragraph. And there is -- let me see whether we have it on the screen. Yes. Here we have a -- what's called a normally reliable source and he provides additional information about the 7th Muslimanske Brigade, and the source confirmed that this brigade is commanded from Zenica with battalions deployed within the 3rd Corps area. "A battalion from the 7th Brigade is deployed on the front line in the Travnik area. Members of the battalion consider themselves Mujahedin in every sense. The majority of members are staunch, practicing Muslims recruited from the local area. Although this particular battalion was instructed by two Iranians, the source confirmed that external Mujahedin from Islamic countries within the brigade numbered at the most 100 to 150. A number of 7th Brigade soldiers on checkpoints north of Vitez were noted wearing a cap badge consisting of a green Muslim crescent insert with a gold star. They stated that this was an insignia for the Muslimanske Brigade." Now, do you remember looking back to that day? Perhaps it's reflected in your diary on your book that a normally reliable source provided this type of information?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it in my diary do you say? I don't think so. I don't remember this, but I accept it's from a milinfosum from my battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm also curious because it says in the first line "additional information." Apparently this source may have, you know -- or the issue was discussed beforehand. Do you have any knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that the two Iranians - and we talk about January now -- already discussed here by this reliable source, you know, they appear to reappear in documents later, and I think we have seen that yesterday. So indeed, that seems to be a reliable source?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I suppose it might have been from the person that wrote this -- this report. I don't want to dispute the authenticity of the military information summary; I just want to say that perhaps because of slackness on my part I didn't see it. I wish someone had shown me this, but I'm sure I didn't see it before it went out. I would have been very interested in this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, my question, you know, how do you assess now your source of information about the comment you made between Mujahedin and the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, I've got a --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you can drink some water.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope it will work. No, I don't change my position with regard to the business of Mujahedin group, and I accept that there are individuals from other countries that come and actually work in the HVO and BiH. I saw quite a number of people from external countries working with the HVO. And it's difficult to define what is a mercenary here and what is a volunteer. And I had a slight difficulty with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that contradicts what this milinfosum, this reliable source says. It says, and I quote again: "A battalion from the 7th Brigade is deployed on the front line in the Travnik area. Members of the battalion consider themselves Mujahedin in every sense." It goes on to make a difference between local and foreign people, and they are all part of this Muslimanske Brigade. Doesn't it say that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does say that. Members of the battalion, presumably, would include locals. Now, they're starting to call themselves Mujahedin. This might be a bit of bravado. I don't know. I accept. I wish I had seen this on the day, the 27th of January I suspect I was still involved with Gornji Vakuf or something, but I accept that this is a report. And I accept that it was sent by my battalion, and I accept that it was probably from a patrol report. That's how we normally get information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just following up what you said, it not only talks about local people considering themselves as Mujahedin, it talks specifically about external Mujahedin from Islamic countries within the brigade and it even gives a number, almost 100 to 150.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when you started talking about numbers, I didn't think it was anything like that, 100 to 150 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in the Mujahedin group or groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in your assessment, how many were there then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was difficult to say, but I saw with my own eyes 15 to 20, no more. And other people reported that it was about 30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were these other people?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: My source.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your basis of information is that one source plus the personal encounter you had at that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and also my offices. I used to talk to them about -- particularly the company commanders about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did discuss the issue with your company commanders?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I discussed it in the 5.00 conference. I can't remember exact details, but we were desperately trying to find out what was happening the whole time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so it was -- would be this type of information you would discuss with your superiors --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- with your subordinates --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this is a mistake on my part not to have seen this. To be honest, it's the first time this week I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were other type of information like that, if you would go through other milinfosums?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's normally me saying I want to know what's going on. Has anyone seen or has anyone had any contact? That sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me conclude with a similar document. It might be indeed one of the milinfosums or one of the issues you discussed with your subordinates in one of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, this is tab 8 in my bundle. It's a milinfosum dated 11th March 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There's a small error in the transcript. The milinfosum that we referred to was 4 -- it said 428 [as interpreted], but it should have been 408 [as interpreted]. I don't know. Wait a moment. There's still an error. It is 98 and not 88. 98. It should be 98.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this witness is another milinfosum. This type it's number 132. Do you recognise it also as a genuine, authentic document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's go to the second page, the bottom of it when it talks about Zepce. And I read it out to you again. "121 Cheshire LO visited both BiH and HVO headquarters in Zepce. Tension has been raised in the town by the arrival of external Muslim forces in the town. Muslim troops reportedly from the 7th Muslim Brigade have moved into house in Zepce. The local commander reported that these troops were not under his direct command and he could not always control their actions. There has been a number of minor incidents in the town involving drunken Muslim soldiers, but the situation is not assessed as serious. Comment. The reason behind a deployment of Muslim externals into the area is not known. The standard 3rd Corps policy is to deploy a brigade," or perhaps that battalion, BN, "or elements of a -- of 7th Brigade to a particular sector of need on the front line or an area of potential Croat/Muslim conflict. However, the deployment of the three troops into potential ethnic conflict areas tends to inflame the situation rather than calm it down. Comment ends." Colonel, do you recall having discussed this influx of external Muslim forces into the town of Zepce at one point in time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that we talked about it at some stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here -- I believe yesterday you said in response to a question -- I think a document was shown to you about originating BH Kiseljak where you said it's like putting petrol into a fire already. Do you agree with me that the comment down here appears to say the same?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Muslim forces, the 3rd Corps used, according to this comment, these forces, external forces, to ignite, inflame the situation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could read it another way. The way I could read it is these people arrived and weren't under the control of the ABiH commander in the area, as is said here. As I feel that these guys -- these Mujahedin -- this Mujahedin group or groups was moving around out of control. Now, here you see a report and it says this time that the local commander commented that troops were not under his command. And to be quite honest, in fairness to the Mujahedin, the drunken Muslim contingent would probably not be them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was the local commander?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Local commander, it says local commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if you look at the second part of the comment it appears to say, at least according to the assessment of this commentator, that this was a deliberate 3rd Corps policy to use these people in a particular sector -- in an area of potential Croat/Muslim conflict for specific purpose. That's what it appears to say?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the standard tactic of any commander when a front is weak is to reinforce it, if necessary, at his decision, perhaps with reservists. And that may be a requirement. I'm not quite sure there's a necessarily -- that actually it says here that the standard policy -- it's the standard policy of any commander to be honest. If you've got a weak part of your line, you may need to reinforce it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But reinforce with a specific unit, the Mujahedin would add a certain flame --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: But in fairness this is a comment -- I'm trying to be fair as well in response to your questioning because I accept your arguments sometimes. The standard 3rd Corps policy is to deploy a battalion or elements of 7th Brigade to a particular sector of lead on the front line. And that would be the standard policy of anyone. It might not be -- that's in comment that -- they didn't know that. That's a comment on the situation. It doesn't come under the factual side of the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was the fair assessment of one of your subordinates on the basis of the facts which were available to him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
