utterances.text: I assume so, and I think I knew about this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who drafted -- made this comment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to refer back to the same sort of general answers I gave before. It may well have been coordinated by my second in command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did ever Mr. Morillon get back to you and say, Stop these stupid comments, you know, they don't help Have you ever about that??

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't. And actually even though they may seem stupid in retrospect, at the time we were doing our best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why are you saying they may look stupid in retrospect?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I don't necessarily agree with them now, you know. But my point is: I was at fault for not seeing every document that went out. I accept that fault. Failure of command, if you like, because I take responsibility for these documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm interested in why you disagree today. What's the basis -- what more information do you have today than the people -- your people had on the ground at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last report, I have a problem with, not this particular one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again my question is: What additional information do you have in relation to the last report to tell today under oath that at that time you thought the report in your opinion was not accurate or whatever your opinion is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one, I didn't see the first report; this report I accept. The first report I didn't see at the time. But my opinion, which hasn't changed, at the time, was that the Mujahedin group was not under operational control of anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the basis for it, just to repeat, is your personal contacts with the Mujahedin at that checkpoint between Zenica and, I think, Zavidovici, and secondly, your source?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And also talking to the soldiers on the ground. Saying, Look, who -- anyone near these people?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are the same soldiers that would be part of information collecting, gathering, providing, so that these comments and assertions could be made?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 900 of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the same soldiers, the information they gave, their information is assessed differently by you today, ten years after the events, and by the persons at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, by me at the time was assessed differently. It remains the same today, as the assessment then. And clearly there were differences in the information we were gathering and consequently the intelligence we were trying to make from it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the only thing reflecting the information level and the assessment your Battalion, the 1st Cheshire Battalion, you and BritBat made at that time is reflected in these milinfosums. Your opinion at that time isn't recorded anywhere.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably correct. Probably correct. I -- we had another chain of command to the British, but we generally did it verbally. It was difficult enough doing a military infosum every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these other chains of information you had with the British, they would end up in London at the end of the day?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we would frequently have disagreements. You know, people -- various commanders had differing views. Everyone's human. My successor would have a different view. Someone else in my position might have a different view. My view was what I stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you agree at the end of the day at one time somewhere on a desk in London the two different information streams could come together, the written milinfosums from your subordinates and your oral comments?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. They -- this one was sent to the -- the United Nations, up the United Nations chain of command. We -- we -- I had a full intelligence section working -- operating in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But again, nobody ever told you, you know, it's very curious. What you tell us is totally different from the milinfosums we are getting from you on a daily basis. Nobody -- either Mr. Morillon or --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's unfair. It's totally different. We've had and I have pointed out there are differences. But the broad thrust of military information summaries is correct. One or two areas - and I've accepted my fault, my responsibility - I didn't see that milinfosum. I remember this incident, and I accept that we weren't perfect. I also accept that it was my viewpoint based on what I was doing at the time. At the time in this period in Bosnia, I wasn't even sure they spent the night in my base most times. I was permanently out, and so a lot of these things were done in my absence. I was on the road either between Gornji Vakuf or in Gornji Vakuf, or up in Turbe. These are vast distances to be covered in an armoured vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the central point where the information was received was in your operational room in your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I accept there was clearly from my perspective things that went wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For instance?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for instance a report that I would disagree with. I mean, I -- we did our best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I very much appreciate your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We come to the re-examination stage. And I look at the Defence attorneys to give them the floor for any re-examination. Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I should just like to know how much time I have before the break to prepare my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The break would normally take place at half past 12.00, so you have 35 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Re-examined by Mr. Bourgon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Sorry for my voice, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me begin by asking you a quick question concerning an issue that was raised by my colleague concerning the distrust amongst people in the former Yugoslavia, amongst the parties. Did you experience the fact that people did not trust each other in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your experience is there one person that you know of that would be trusted by all sides?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Merdan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why is that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he was well-known by everyone and because he had honour and decency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you provide the Trial Chamber with an example where you saw that General Merdan was trusted more than another person?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I first went, Your Honours, to Bosnia, one of the real problems was that we had an outbreak of fighting in Vitez and Donji -- Novi Travnik. And I went in -- I only had Land Rovers. I had no soldiers. But it seemed to me that we had to stop the fighting otherwise the United Nations couldn't deploy. So I drove into Novi Travnik and I first went to the headquarters of a man called -- I think he was called Lendo. And he had taken six HVO soldiers as prisoners or hostages. So I demanded that I have them and take them back before I went to see the HVO. He refused point-blank. So I said, Okay, I'll just take one as proof that you're going to look after them. And he said, Yes. My point was when I got -- when I went across town, there was still fight -- it wasn't a good situation. There was still a lot of fire fight around. I met Kordic in a bar -- I think it was called something like the Grand Bazaar or something. He was upstairs. And I said, This fighting has got to stop now otherwise the UN can't deploy, I can't carry out my operational role. Please, actually, let's have a cease-fire. And I said, Who would you like to speak to on the other side for the ABiH. And Kordic said, Only Dzemal Merdan, and I had never met Merdan at this point. We got on a satellite phone. We drafted a cease-fire agreement. And then I went to go and get Merdan from Zenica and we started our meeting at 2.00 in the morning and finished it at 4.00 with a kind of agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Did you know what was the position of General Merdan at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't sure at the time, but it was soon apparent that he was something to do with the 3rd Corps and probably the deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know, Colonel, when the 3rd Corps was actually created?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know where was General Hadzihasanovic in September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I met him then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much information did you have at that time on the 3rd Corps itself and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its units?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to bring you to a document which was used by my colleague yesterday which is part of your diary when you recalled a briefing that was given to you in Zagreb. Do you recall this briefing discussed yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And yesterday you said that you were told by an individual that most people in Bosnia and Herzegovina are really good at twisting the truth and that all parties are quite prepared to attack their own people and to blame it on someone else.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having spent nine months in Central Bosnia, do you agree with this statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes and no. Yes insofar as I'm sure there were people capable of doing such a disgusting thing; and no, the vast majority of people would not, HVO, ABiH, and the Bosnian Serb army, and the Mafia of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would a comment like this apply to General Merdan?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it would not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would a comment like that apply in your experience to General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it certainly did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Lieutenant Colonel Doyle, I believe, provide any basis for his remark when you were in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he -- he -- I think he was Lord Owen's or Lord Carrington's special advisor. So we almost took it down verbatim what he was saying because we knew nothing. So I wrote it down and reported it in my diary and indeed I reported in my situation report to my battle group when I got back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you think it was proper for the head of the European Community Monitoring Mission in Bosnia to make such derogatory comments about the population in Bosnia as you were about to deploy to save their lives?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he didn't make them. Doyle was a staff officer, and the answer is: That was an opinion and this is a private diary, and I think it's perfectly proper for him to prefer his opinion if that's the way he felt. Later I was to discover that that wasn't necessarily the case. But at the time, I accepted it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it possible, Colonel, that what Lieutenant Colonel Doyle wanted to do at that time was really to say, Guys, be careful and don't take anything for granted?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the lesson I got from it. Because from then on one of the maxims I worked by was that I never believed anything, Your Honours, that anyone said to me until I saw evidence of what they said happening on the ground. And it was almost a principal maxim that I applied to the way I operated. When I see actions on the ground, I believe what -- you know, mentally I would say, then I'll believe you're doing it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you say whether you saw such action -- whenever there was a commitment by General Hadzihasanovic, did you see such action on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be quite honest, if I didn't with both Hadzihasanovic and with Merdan -- with Blaskic I would be hammering on the door rather quickly, which I did on occasion. But it takes a while to get instructions down from the top, particularly in the situation of lack of communication. No telephones, for example, it's difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the fact that one night you showed up at General Hadzihasanovic's headquarters and you requested a cease-fire for 6.00, and we saw yesterday the order imposing a cease-fire on his troops, is that an example of what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I -- I didn't see that written order. I don't think I saw it at the time. So it was done blind to me. But yes, there's an example. And then actually if it's not this occasion, another occasion when it hadn't happened, I would go back and demand that I need some assistance to make sure it did happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you requested that checkpoint in Kacuni to be turned down, to be taken out, and we saw yesterday the order issued by General Hadzihasanovic, is that the type of incident you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the 3rd Corps follow through with your request, albeit with difficulty?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I felt for these commanders, Your Honours. I mean, it's not like, you know, you could just pick up a phone and speak to them. Sometimes they had to wait for the commander to come back to a telephone for contact to be made. It was very difficult indeed, but the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to -- since we are on the issue of Kacuni, I have a few questions with respect to what happened. First I'd like to refer to you -- you mentioned that two persons were killed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was reminded that two persons were killed, but, you know, there was a lot happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'd like you -- to refer you to your diary, and that is on the 26th of January. And this is on page 0890, I believe at the end. And it's the first paragraph on 26th of January dealing with the Kacuni roadblock.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, here we are. It's in my diary. You're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us from reading this paragraph or, if you recall, in what circumstances those two persons were killed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly how they were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that information that was relayed to you or were you witness to those killings?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I certainly was not witness to the killings, and it would be information that was relayed to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those killings that you were informed of, would they have happened after the 21st of January according to the information that you received?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If they are mentioned in this incident on the 26th?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's likely that they were just before the incident of the 26th, but I don't know exactly when they were killed. I suspect it was the 25th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I showed you a document yesterday, and that was document number 9 in the binder that you had yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this document you acknowledged with me what had happened on the 21st, which is that between 8.00 and 9.00 on the 20th of January the HVO put a checkpoint at the entry and at the exit of the town. And then they pounded the town between 9.00 and 2.00 in the morning and then removed the checkpoints. I refer here to document DH612. Now, with this in mind, when you look back to your diary to the comment that you made to General Merdan where you told him, and I quote: "I told him that this time the Muslims were at least in some way to blame. They had killed two HVO personnel and they were holding me up."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In context can you explain what was the problem at that time and what you meant by "at least in some way this time."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I tried, Your Honours, to always stay neutral. It was very difficult, because to act is to destroy neutrality on the ground. And people -- as soon as you do one thing, people -- the other side thinks you're supporting. So I was trying to be neutral, and I never necessarily blamed people, but in this case I said it seems you were responsible, so that is what I meant: It seems that by your actions of soldiers you have killed two people, and this is actually causing an absolute problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the difficulty to you was that they were holding you up?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they -- my main objective in that area was to keep the main supply route into Kiseljak and thence into Sarajevo, the ground route, open. That's what I considered to be an objective of mine because it was the only route into Sarajevo for foodstuffs, medicines, et cetera. So to hold me up, what I meant was to stop me actually sending aid convoys into Sarajevo through Kiseljak. And this was the only route and this was the only way I could get in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the roadblock, was that what the ABiH was doing wrong at that time in your view?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because they were blocking -- they were stopping a UN mission and in fact they were also stopping us patrolling that area, but not just that. There was an agreement -- we all agreed to try and keep the routes open. So that was a problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you recalled -- you said yesterday that this incident was solved by you placing two warriors to replace this lorry with the logs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- well, that was my suggested solution, and I left those vehicles in position for at least several days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you decide to leave two warriors? What was the aim and who could pass from then on, at that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I left the warriors to reassure the people who had put the barricade up, because I think also it was relatively close to the HVO front line positions. So the people who lived there, who seemed to be Bosnian Muslims in the main, were reassured by actually having our presence. And this was a tactic I used time and time again, to put my soldiers into a position where people felt frightened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you understand what the use of the checkpoint was to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military aim of that checkpoint was to deny communication between Kiseljak and Vitez for the HVO and also to provide a reassurance for the people who lived in that area. And by default, it stopped us moving up and down the road, too, particularly when you put the -- the lorry was huge. It had great trunks on the back, and it stretched right across the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And once you, meaning the international community, could have freedom of movement again in this particular area, for you the issue was solved?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except, you know, I wanted people not to be fighting there. So solved insofar as we opened the road, so that's correct. But I still would have prefer people not to be at each other's throats. In fact I got -- at Kacuni I got attacked as well. My interpreter lost the toe -- his toe cap.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You beat me to the question. I just wanted to know who was your interpreter. I believe that I see from the diary that (redacted) was with you. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was known as (redacted) because we tried to disguise his identity. He was a British Serb officer and we also had a British 25 Serb sergeant. So we changed their names, not very subtly, to (redacted) and (redacted), but it was (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is he the person you are talking about when you say that the only casualty it was the top of (redacted) boot, which was struck by something?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move on, Colonel, to the issue of the -- the role of the adjutant which was raised yesterday by my colleague. Can you explain what is normally the rank of the adjutant in a battalion. Who normally gets this position, and what are the duties of the adjutant?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: The adjutant is a captain in rank. He's normally perhaps one of the best if not the best captain in the battalion, and his duty is to run the battalion apart from the training and the operations. In all other aspects his staff job is to run a battalion under the commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we compare the position of the adjutant to that of a G1 in a brigade, would there be a difference or would they resemble each other?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would resemble one another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Can you tell the Trial Chamber what the G1 does in a brigade?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: He runs things like discipline, education, that sort of thing, and the re-positions of units out of combat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to move now, Colonel, to the issue of Dusina. Now, my colleague -- first let me ask you the first question. If after an investigation no crime is committed, did you expect anyone to provide you information that someone can be court martialed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would have liked that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's be clear. A lot of people were dying at this time, Your Honours, including my own escort driver had been shot and I was demanding that we have the person responsible -- I hadn't even got an investigation for what had happened to my own driver. But I was -- didn't stop me demanding -- for every single crime committed, I wanted to know what was going on. So the answer to the question is: Did I receive good information that somebody had been disciplined? The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that following the meeting in Dusina, that following the series of meetings that took place - I'm not going to go back into those meetings - but correct me if I'm wrong, you said that you were satisfied that this incident was closed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that. Closed insofar as I couldn't do anything about it. I couldn't be responsible for everyone dying in the area, although I felt it quite personally that it was part of my mission to try and stop it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... one of your answers in the Kordic case, you mentioned that Merdan told you that the people concerned were going to be court-martialed, then it would not be the persons in Dusina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The issue of Merdan mentioning this to you, did that -- did this happen once or many times?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several times. Several times when I complained, General Merdan said something would be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me move on to the issue of the Geneva Conventions. Would you agree with me - and just to confirm with what my colleague said to you - that it is a duty of a commanding officer to instruct his troops on the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the basis of the document I showed you yesterday as to whether saying that there was an order out and the corps commander to instruct the units on the applicable law, is that a way for the corps commander to ensure that the person -- that his soldiers as best as possible will be trained in the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very good way of doing that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you expect or would you expect, Colonel, to see General Hadzihasanovic holding classes on the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't. But I would expect General Hadzihasanovic to have done what he did, tell people -- refer them to the fact that the ABiH must act in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. And if people don't understand what those are, perhaps to explain them further. But I expect the officers to whom General Hadzihasanovic was addressing looked to the Geneva Conventions, totally understood what the Geneva Conventions were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, the -- we looked at the issue of the -- an order which was issued by Colonel Blaskic. My friend showed you this order, and I guess you may still have the order with you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we -- may the usher please bring the exhibit which was shown to the witness dated 18th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I ask you, Colonel, just to tell you what exactly is meant by paragraph 1 of this order from Kordic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: First of all, we are no longer in examination-in-chief, and we are also not in cross-examination. It's re-examination. And I didn't object yesterday when my learned friend, you know, had him comment on what Mr. Hadzihasanovic intended, what did he do, what did he mean by that. But here now in re-examination, it's really of no use to ask him what did he mean, Mr. Blaskic, when he issued this order. It speaks for itself and he can only speculate, and that's of no use for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you well, this document was issued on the 18th of April, 1993. It was at 8.00 in the morning, and it is marked by "urgent, urgent, urgent." Is that the case? This document was shown to the witness as a new exhibit, and the question was also put to the witness within the context of cross-examination. And the question that was put to the witness now wants to be clarified by the Defence. You may proceed, Mr. Bourgon, but in the sense that I have indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Mr. President. Because the question that I'm going to put the witness -- I'm just the Defence counsel, but I really did not understand any of the questions put to the witness by the Prosecution and I would like to clarify some issues that remained unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 1 of this order, what is your interpretation as to what is being asked by this order?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stop UN vehicles moving into an operational area. Pursuant, Your Honours, worries me. I wonder if that's an exact translation, because it could mean pursuant after reference to the orders of a superior commander. Could be that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anything in this document, Colonel, that is giving an order to fire at the UN?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it gives clearance to fire in some way or another if there's a requirement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But to deliberately fire. Is that what this order is giving?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say -- the final paragraph contradicts everything, arbitrary behaviour -- well, slightly contradicts. What does he mean by arbitrary behaviour, number 5?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that confirm, Colonel, what you were saying that in your view no one had been given orders to shoot at the UN?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could do, but this is a very confusing order to me. If I received it in the English like this, I would demand clarification as to what exactly is meant. So I suspect in the original Croatian it would be clearer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now, the issue that was raised along with the questions related to this document was the issue of control. Now, can you state in terms of controlling the troops what you mean by "troops out of control within the army."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I particularly mean, Your Honours, a man who is in a probably location up the front line who is frightened, who is bored, who actually has no one near him, who decides to open fire without orders and without reason. A sniper position maybe. And that is, I think, the position of the person that killed my escort driver on the 30th of January, and there were various other instance. And that was by the -- in my view, in my opinion, came from an area controlled by the ABiH; therefore, it was an ABiH soldier out of control. And in my view, there were other soldiers out of control in -- on all sides. I'd give an example on the other side. A HVO soldier attacking my petrol dump in a drive-past shoot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, the -- on the 18th of April, where were you yourself and what is the context of this order?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Zenica. I went into Vitez. I lost a vehicle -- it overturned behind me on the return back. I took -- I see -- I chaired a cease-fire meeting. I made a plan to try and patrol Vitez and arrange for armoured vehicles to be positioned in the town. And I arranged for a joint commission to investigate what was happening. I went to the International Committee of the Red Cross to make ensure that they were happy about prisoner exchange. And for the first time the International Committee of the Red Cross travelled in one of our armoured vehicles with permission from Geneva. And I noticed there were 16 bodies on my route from Vitez. That was all I wrote on that day

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I'd like, just before the break, to ask you -- and you've spoke about that in your examination-in-chief and you also provided some more information to my colleague in his cross-examination. But can you tell us -- you've just read us one day. Can you tell us what you were doing most of the time during your mission in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of my time, Your Honours, I was away from my base. I had two, three vehicles. I had an armoured vehicle, a kind of light tank called a Warrior. The foreign office -- the British foreign office gave me a Land Rover Discovery, a Land Rover, white. I had another Land Rover as well, another Land Rover fitted for radios and I would spend most of my time actually on the ground often at frontline positions like Turbe, Maglaj, and if I wanted to visit Tuzla, that took me a minimum of seven hours to get there, and I had a company base up there. And if I wanted to visit Gornji Vakuf, that took me a minimum of two hours to get there. So most of my time I was away from my headquarters. For that reason I appointed two operations officers so that 24 by 7 I would have someone of my own -- actually, I don't mean to say anyone else was alien, but someone -- an operations officer knew exactly what I was doing and what I wanted to do. They were put in the operations room. They were captains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how would you decide on a certain day what the focus of your attention would be?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the night-before's conference I would receive reports as to what was happening and I would decide where the point of everyone's -- well, certainly my concentrated efforts should be the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the time that you spent in Central Bosnia, how many other people have travelled as much as you did and have made as many observations as you did about the main incidents that were going on?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. A lot of the liaison officers, I had appointed six liaison officers to get to know the area extremely well and gave them sectors to govern. I should think that the liaison officers were out as much as I was, if not more. They used to spend time actually sleeping with the units on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you feel, Colonel, that your way you operated allowed you to understand and to know what was going on despite the vastness of your area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, no one -- no one gave me instructions. I've been to staff college and things. No one gave me instructions on how to operate in this extraordinary place. So I did my best, and that fundamentally meant working out how to operate as we went. Obviously I got things wrong, like the Prosecution has identified. I did not -- I was not systematic enough with the military information summaries; I accept that. But my style of command was that I would be with the soldiers on the ground as much as possible and talking to the relevant commanders as often as I could and fundamentally being at the position -- in a position to make a decision in time to stop people dying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one last question before the break, Colonel. My friend has shown you a number of milinfosum -- actually, maybe two, maybe three at the most, which he discussed with you in relation to alleged control over Mujahedin. And we'll go after the break into these documents very quickly just to ask you a few questions, but how many more milinfosums to your knowledge in the complete period when you were there for your BritBat 1 and operation Grapple 1 contained information related to Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it's easy as I've never read them. But I would suspect that the people who -- preparing for this trial have been through them with a tooth comb, I suspect there aren't many other -- other military information summaries ones that contain references to the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you say that the information that you had at the time, if I asked you, was it plenty, was it middle, or was it almost nonexistent? Where does it come closer on the Mujahedin issue?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what, I would have liked to have actually met them properly. So I would think that I had to -- I would be in the middle or towards the lower end of middle of lack of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, after the break we'll go into some of the questions that my colleague asked you, the Mujahedin, and then I'll be finished with my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe this is a good time from the break. I have another 20 minutes after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that in line 8, page 76, there is a mistake in the transcript. In English it says my friend has shown you a number. You're referring to the Prosecution, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Prosecution, they are my friends. Of course. I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to make a break. It is 25 to 1.00 and we are going to resume around 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. The Prosecution wishes to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, just one brief point, if Mr. Bourgon could indicate how long his re-direct lasts because you don't need to be reminded but this re-direct comes in on cross. So whatever this witness says, I have no chance to follow-up. So he should really limit himself, as we are in chief and in cross-examination to the most important issues. And I don't know how long he's intending to go on, but I just wanted to make this observation, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. As I said just before the break, I need roughly another 20 minutes. All my questions are directly linked to the examination of my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because the Prosecution cannot take the floor again unless you open up some new questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... before the break, and in your last answer, I believe, was that the information you had on Mujahedin during your tour from the mid to the on lower end. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't have much information about the Mujahedin, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My colleague has shown you a document which was at tab 7 in the documents that were given to you, and that was the interview between a journalist that I believe you know, Andrew Hogg, and an individual pretending to be a Mujahedin. I'd like to refer you to this document. Now, my colleague has shown you some lines, and I would also like to do the same thing to see if this document which was shown to you by my colleague --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't want to be picky, but I don't think there's evidence that this person was pretending to be a Mujahedin. All the evidence we have is that he is, that's what he says, a Mujahedin. So I object to the word "pretending." It's also suggestive to this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The remark has been well-noted, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but first let me ask you, where were you in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Germany, Fahlenbostel [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever informed of the existence of an individual named Abdul Aziz?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given the -- the text that was given to you I would like to refer you to some of the lines and do the exact same exercise as my colleague did and say -- find out whether this reinforces your belief or not concerning the existence of Mujahedin in Central Bosnia. Now, I refer you to page 2 at the top where this is an answer provided by this gentleman Aziz. And he said about: "About myself or my group, it is not allowed to come through any official [inaudible] organisation or any government involvement. My people, they are coming by themselves, by their own efforts. Nobody is forcing them or nobody is requesting them. They just heard like me that there are Muslims being killed and they should help." Does that reinforce your belief that there is no link between the 3rd Corps and the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really have a comment. I believe that from what I knew this looks to be support and -- but I don't change my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to be sure about re-direct. It's not asking leading questions. He can ask him what his comment about that, but we have to be careful at this point in time. But I'm curious what the gentleman says about this sentence, but procedurally I believe we have to be careful the way it's phrased.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The same procedure has been used as that of my colleague. During my re-direct, I show him the same document. He has the document in front of him and I am asking him to comment on it. This is not a new procedure, but I can understand that my colleague wants to object. It's quite legitimate on his part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: My objection was to the phrasing of the question. It's the same document, but I was cross-examining and you're examining or examining in-chief. You're not supposed to ask leading questions, and you asked one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Make sure that the questions are not leading, but you're reading a paragraph and asking him what he thinks about it. So the question is not leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, the paragraph I just read to you, and maybe we can read it again, saying that this individual -- saying that, and I quote the paragraph: "My people, they are coming by themselves, by their own efforts. Nobody is forcing them, nobody is requesting them, and they just heard like me that there are Muslims being killed and they should help." Can you comment on this paragraph with respect to the question that was posed to you and the control of Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the assumption I made that so many people arrived in Bosnia. It -- in one way it certainly does confirm that -- from my point of view that they weren't asked for because my impression, and it was an impression, that these people just arrived -- these Mujahedin just arrived as a group. But as individuals, it's much more understandable. A lot of people used to arrive at places like Split seeking adventure or whatever purpose and joined there the relevant armed forces from there as individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, I now refer you to page 5 of the same document towards the bottom of the page. This is a reply by the gentleman named Aziz, and he is saying: "They are coming through different area. There is no specific area they are coming." And again the same thing, "I will never ask them how you arrived there. And the journalist you know, Hogg, is replying: "So what you are saying there is no organisation in the Islamic world sending people here?" And the response by Mr. Aziz is "neither." The question is the same: "How does that relate, if it does, to your opinion, that the Mujahedin were not under control?"

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't asked for them and they came as they wished. I am sure that's what I feel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I now refer you to page 7 of the same document. And this is a question that was asked to Mr. Aziz by Mr. Hogg, and that's the second paragraph. And the question goes as follows: "Yeah. What has been the reception that you receive from Izetbegovic and the Bosnian government? Did they welcome you with open arms or did it take a lot of negotiating to be able to?" Mr. Aziz butting in and answering: "No. Especially by Muslims, yes. They opened their hands and we are welcome and they even help us with any kind of -- they have food or anything because they recognise that we are here to defend them." This question and answer, does that indicate to you or how does that relate to your opinion that those Mujahedin were not under control of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it indicates either way that answer actually, but my reflection is that the Bosnian Muslims were under such pressure at that time, I often used to think maybe they would -- this is privately at the time and since, but certainly at the time I used to think, Poor devils. They -- there's no one really supporting them. So they might accept help from any direction, and any direction, I meant by this people coming to help them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I finally refer you to page 12 of the same document. And again this is a question by Mr. Hogg saying: "From countries, governments, or from the individuals." And the response is: "No. Individuals, no. No single country giving us from other. It is from government, but we are getting help from all these personal effort." How does that relate to your opinion of Mujahedin and control?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the same as before, people were coming of their own will. I also would like to comment maybe the Mujahedin unit came as a complete entity, I don't know. But my point was, I don't think they were under control of the ABiH. I don't know how they got there. They might have dribbled in like this or they might have come as a unit. But my point is, as far as I could see, they weren't under control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, when I look at this interview that was conducted in 1992, does it really help you in making up your mind, one way or the other, with Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't change my view, but it's interesting from my point of view -- I didn't realise there was so many Middle East people in the area from as early as that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, I'd like to show you a document and I'd like the usher to take out Exhibit DH181. Now, this is a piece written by the same journalist and I'd like you to take a look at this same document. This is written by Andrew Hogg that you know. And because he was looking for the same information, I think it's good that you look at this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be placed on the ELMO. Can the document be placed on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO, and it's DH181.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you -- maybe I will help you to read some of the sentences. And if I begin initially at the beginning: "Senior Bosnian army commanders are calling on their president Alija Izetbegovic to expel foreign Mujahedin fighters because they are terrorising civilians and committing atrocities. More than 200 Mujahedin who have been fighting in Bosnia for the past year now operate as lawless gangs which the Bosnian army command is powerless to control. In recent clashes between Croats and Muslims, the Islamic soldiers who say they are waging jihad, holy war, have desecrated churches and murdered civilians. When they are not fighting the Mujahedin have terrified the population they claim to defend by attempting to enforce an Islamic code on a population traditionally lax about religious observance. Colonel Stipan Siber, deputy commander of the Bosnia Hercegovina army and its operations chief in Central Bosnia said last week the freelance fighters were causing widespread alarm. It was a mistake to let them in. No one asked them to come. They commit most of the atrocities. They worked against the interest of the Muslim people." I'll let you take a quick look at the rest of this document, Colonel, and tell me if this can relate to your opinion that the Bosnian -- that the Mujahedin were not under the control of the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it confirms what my thoughts were. And he's a good journalist, this man. So I presume he'd done good research. I notice Miletici is mentioned and that's an interesting second back-up to the fact that it might have been Mujahedin who did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I'd like to move now to a document which was shown to you which was at tab number 9 in the list of documents by my colleague, and that is one of the milinfosums. Is that 9 or -- yes, sorry. It's not a milinfosum. This is a document that is labelled P461. Now, my first question to you, Colonel, is that: Have you ever seen this document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have never seen the document before today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you confirm that with respect to the 7th Brigade you had very little information?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I had little information about the 7th Brigade. I mean, my intelligence cell may have had more, but I didn't carry information in my head about the 7th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you aware of what is mentioned into this document, which is that there are some foreign citizens who are being detained?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I wasn't aware but I know there were a lot of foreign citizens, so-called, actually in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in this document you have before you do you see anywhere the term "3rd Corps"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the top.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of the reporting of the document, does that tell you anything that those people were members of the 3rd Corps, or if they were members of anything it was the BH army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no mention of the 3rd Corps, but we're talking about the area in which the 3rd Corps operated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these two individuals that were referred to by my colleague Skinner and McBride, would they qualify as foreign citizens who are members of the BH army, i.e., volunteers who are in our unit?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the incident of the -- what happened to Skinner and McBride, how does that contribute -- did that contribute in any way to you forming an opinion about the control of Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did actually. It was -- perhaps I should have mentioned it before but you remind me. The death of -- Your Honours, the death of McBride and Skinner upset me a great deal because I had had personal contact with these men. I had tried to get them out of the place as I told them to go, as I told all mercenaries, and I considered them to be mercenaries, to get out. And because I knew them personally, I was upset. I spent some time thinking and talking, why would the BiH do it to their own? And the answer and the conclusion I made and others made was that they were actually killed by a Mujahedin group for reasons presumably that they were Westerners, Christians whatever you want do. I know when I went to their burials, I assume they were Christians because I took their torbay [phoen], the headstones off and put crosses instead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the way in which they were killed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that they were killed somewhere near Turbe. They were taken out of their houses in the middle of the night. They were taken, and their bodies were found in a stream and they were shot in the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember exactly shot where or how, or did that contribute to your -- to giving you any information with respect to Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- I think it was near Travnik and we felt that it was a Mujahedin unit that had done it. And I think it might have been done during the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the number of bullets used to kill these two individuals?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- in my mind it's 17, but in other words over ten. A burst of fire in the back of the jacket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll now move to tab number 11 which was raised to you. This is document P626. And I -- my question to you, Colonel, first is: Did you ever see this document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not before this week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us who this document is addressed to and who is the person sending this document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I think this is the HVO command in Mostar and sending to the 9th of March -- that's about it. I don't know quite more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a document that you would have access -- that you would have had access to during your stay in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not. It's an internal army document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was such information about existence of 250 Mujahedin, is that information that was ever conveyed to you by anyone during your stay in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll now move to tab number 6, another document which was shown to you by my friend, and this is the milinfosum dated 27 January. It was a new document. Now, with respect to this milinfosum which was on the 27th of January, we discussed yesterday a meeting that took place on the 26th with a cease-fire, a meeting that took place on the 27th with a cease-fire, a very serious -- and these two meetings that you attended personally are not reported in this document. Should it have been or what is your view with respect to making these documents reliable for the day whether important events such as this should have been mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it should have been mentioned, but are what these reportings -- you know, it's selective. I mean, I -- as -- as is obvious from the record I was chairing meetings during this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would your battalion have known that you were doing so?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course they would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I look at this document and I want to use that for the -- in terms of -- discuss what was raised with you with my colleague about the milinfosum. Now, if I look at the first page where it says: "Gornji Vakuf was reported to be generally quiet." Now, what does that mean, it "was reported to be" in terms of milinfosum language?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reported generally means we're relying on other sources. "Generally quiet" means there wasn't too much gunfire or shells landing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And reported, what kind of observation would that refer to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could well be that it was reported not by my patrols but by someone else. But I would think it's quite -- this is reported in this sense as I had B company there, it came from B Company's situation report. So as they're right beside the town, they can hear explosions and shooting from where they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I look at page 2 of this document, the top part where it says that the "BiH and HVO in Travnik have signed an agreement." Is there a difference between this type of language and the first type where it says "it was reported that"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would suspect that Travnik -- this was a report submitted by the liaison officer for Travnik, Captain Matthew Dundas Whatley whose task was to liaise with the BiH and HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you compare the two types of reporting where it says "was reported to be" and the other paragraph, is the second one not a fact and the first one an observation of which we don't know the source?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the writing, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this paragraph that was shown to you where it talks about a normally reliable source, do you yourself know this source?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many sources were used to draft a milinfosum?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: As many as we got information from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what would be a normally reliable source?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this kind of definition is someone in the ranks of either the HVO or the BiH who was friendly and who talked to some of our patrols -- or the liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in this case, in this specific scenario, could the source be a civilian or an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could it be someone that could confuse a soldier wearing a beard with a foreigner?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe. Maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the fact that a battalion would be trained by two people from the outside, is that a sign that an external country is controlling this unit?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. What it means -- what someone being trained, it's -- it -- two people can't train a battalion anyway, Your Honours. But it does actually mean that instruction is being -- is apparently being given by instructors from outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And has the British army ever called upon experts from other countries to come and assist with the training of their troops?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure it has. I'm absolutely sure it has.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to tab number 8, which is the other milinfosum that was shown to you. And this -- the paragraph about Zepce. And this is again a new document which is not yet into evidence. Now, this paragraph with Zepce, first of all as you noted correctly, and maybe you can confirm that and ensure that I'm not getting it wrong, but you would be surprised that the Muslim externals would be those found drunk in the street. I guess you made a comment around that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did make that comment because there were a lot of very bad Muslims in the BiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they drank a lot. They all drank too much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when I look at the first sentence where it says that the local commander, in the middle, he says that "these troops were not under his direct command." Now, what could that mean? Is it a possibility that it's simply another group of BiH soldiers and they are under his operational control and not his operational command?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is a reference to the fact that this group were not taking orders from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there many possibilities as to what this group could or could not be?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is possible that the ABiH had special forces, and in fact I know they had some special forces but -- and they might not take control -- command -- operational control from a local commander. So there is a possibility of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there is the word -- the reference here to the word "external," where it says: "A deployment of Muslim externals." And I'd like to refer you to document we saw yesterday, and this document was the milinfosum of 26 January and it was at tab 14 of the documents I showed you. Now, I'd like to, if you have this document with you, tab 14, it's milinfosum 87. It was a new document dated 26th of January. Now, I'd like to read the last paragraph where it says that B Company stated that the main problem area is the village of Bizlica [phoen] where UN vehicles were still being engaged by HVO snipers as were the local populace, predominantly Muslim. It was also reported that there had been no evidence as of yet of external forces withdrawing out of the local area. This includes the 305th Jajce Brigade. Information leads us to believe that the 305th Brigade moved to the area north of Gornji Vakuf centred on the village of Hranca shortly after the fall of Jajce. Comment. It is now believed that the brigade may be moved to Zenica as it falls in the category of external forces." Looking at this paragraph, what was the word "external forces" used for in milinfosum language?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you -- we've got word play here and it's soldiers writing this report, Your Honour. I think in this context external forces, as I recall -- because I brokered the cease-fire there, that forces not directly from the area of Gornji Vakuf were to be withdrawn from the area. So external in this case probably means a brigade that was not from the Gornji Vakuf area. And I think -- seem to recall that that was the kind of language we used to withdraw -- to calm down the situation by removing the forces on all sides. So this was not referring to external, out of the country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I go back to the document which was seen by my -- which was shown to you by my colleague which talks about the external Muslims, it's quite possible that we are not talking about Mujahedin at all. That's the document -- the new document at milinfosum 132 of 11 March.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite possible. There were some external fanatics, individual fanatics, on all sides. And I can remember particularly one very fanatical HVO soldier from Canada.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, if I look at this incident which you said in answer to a question by my colleague that you were aware of the incident, do you recall that this incident involved Mujahedin at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which incident?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The incident in Zepce where the liaise officer visited the headquarters and we saw those people drunk in the street.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I was aware of the incident. I wasn't aware that it was necessarily Mujahedin at the time -- retrospectively now I suspect there might be, but I wasn't actually going that detailed at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to your source, Colonel, you mentioned that -- and my colleague asked you many questions with respect to your source. And the questions I'd like to ask you are quite simple --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can we move into the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there anybody in the public gallery [as interpreted] or not? Is there anybody after us in the courtroom? Go on, Mr. Bourgon, quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in answer to a question posed to you by my colleague, you mentioned that a commander is responsible to take action for his soldiers. My question to you is very simple: If they are not his soldiers, such as the Mujahedin, and they've done the things that you are aware of, what do you expect the commander to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. That's a mischaracterisation of the facts. That's a mere assumption by my learned friend that they are not his soldiers. He can ask something -- although, again that should have been part of his examination-in-chief. He can ask him, like I did, without any reference to any facts, Mujahedin soldiers. And he's certainly entitled to do that. But now to mix it in again to soldiers, Mujahedin, I think isn't of assistance to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question as it has been put -- if I had the time, I would rephrase it and put it to the witness. The witness himself has touched upon this issue, and this issue would merit more time. Go ahead and put your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and bearing in mind your opinion that the Mujahedin were not under his control and yet the Mujahedin did things you are aware of, what did you expect General Hadzihasanovic to do?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he wasn't responsible for them if he was not in command and control of them, I would expect him to establish, if he doesn't already know, what exactly their right to be there is by reference to a higher formation. I would -- if I was him, I would have an urgent consultation with the chief of police, because if they're not under his operational control, under whose control are they? And if they're under no one's control, perhaps it's a police matter, which actually was one of the things that Merdan used to say to me by chance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I'd like to end this re-examination by showing you one document, that is DH73. I would ask the usher to show you this document and whether this type of action by General Hadzihasanovic would fit into the category of what you would have expected him to do in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I would just like to see the document first before the witness gives his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 73. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, could you read this document -- maybe I will read it for the record. Letter addressed from the commander of the 3rd Corps, General Hadzihasanovic, to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina army staff commander, Mr. Delic, and army staff chief, Mr. Halilovic. And the letter goes as follows: "In the general area of Zenica municipality since the beginning of the war there have been volunteers from foreign countries, Arabs and Turks, as well as a group of Bosnians trained by them, the so-called guerrillas who do not enter -- who have not entered the ranks of the BH army in spite of being invited to. They are still contemplating the proposals made to them by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina army's chief of staff. They do not want to make public the decision regarding their actions and eventual entry into the RBH army's ranks and wish to communicate exclusively with top officials of the RBH army staff and not with the 3rd Corps commander, whose only duty in their opinion is to arrange for them a meeting with the said people. They were in this territory even before the formation of the 3rd Corps. In fighting to date, they have been acting outside the usual context and lawful matters of combat, which is directly detrimental to the BH state and especially to the RBH army. It is a known fact that some state organs and high-ranking Muslim clergymen are behind them. Since negotiations have started and finding a solution with the same at the highest level of the RBH army in order to urgently continue and resolve them," then something is missing, "in this connection I am requesting your stances and opinions regarding the solution to this problem since these units are situated in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps and I do not want to be held accountable for the consequences of their actions." Colonel, is that a kind of actions that you would have expected the commander of the 3rd Corps to take with this problem of these-called Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, that is an exoneration. That is a clear indication that these Mujahedin were not under command or control. It's a request for support from the high command of the ABiH, and it's a request for them to direct how he is to deal with this matter. And quite honestly, this is a matter of strategy at a higher level than corps level. So this is an exoneration of Enver Hadzihasanovic in my view.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, just one last question. In the last paragraph you see that there are -- part of the sentence is in capital letters. Is this a normal way in terms of staff duties in the military to send letters to your superior officers and to highlight some parts in capital letters?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not because that's really emphasising that you are to direct me -- you must direct me, it's a plea for help, in service -- staff duty terms. It's an actually: Don't ignore this and maybe he's actually, by implication, by this asked for advice before this letter and hasn't received it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This closes my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have about ten minutes of questions arising from the cross-examination. I note the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is that if you take ten minutes it will be 2.00 and there is a session after us. If we can't do anything else, go ahead. The Judges won't have any questions, so we'll finish at 2.00, I suppose, unless the Prosecution believes that they have more questions. In that case, we will delay everything until tomorrow morning. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, in light of the last document, which again should have been a document showed in examination-in-chief, I have a few documents to ask him to put it into perspective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time will you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, no more than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't want to waste time, but there's no reason why should the Prosecution be allowed to put any questions following my questions unless their questions have to do with the responsibility of the commander. I have not departed in the least from the cross-examination, and I don't know why the Prosecution should be allowed to put any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution, what do you have to say? They say they have not departed from the cross-examination when it comes to the responsibilities of the commander. What do you think about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I said at the outset, Mr. President, and I believe Mr. Bourgon said he would take 20 minutes and he's almost an hour now. As said that he's going into areas which I might feel we have to cross-examine again, and now he shows a document which hasn't been touched neither by him nor by the Prosecution in cross-examination, and asks him almost an ultimate question as to the ultimate issue of the trial, which is really up to Your Honours to decide. I just want to ask him whether he was aware of a few of the facts which occurred after the document was signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the Defence has shown a new document to the witness, the Prosecution is expected to reply. If Mr. Dixon takes his ten minutes and if after that the Prosecution goes on to examine for five minutes, that will take us to ten minutes past 2.00. Okay. Let's go and do it. Mr. Dixon, very quickly, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Further cross-examination by Mr. Dixon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were shown a number of documents by the Prosecution at the brigade level of the 3rd Corps. Just so we can be absolutely clear on this point, can you confirm that you had never seen any of those brigade documents before?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it would be correct then, would it not, that you cannot comment on whether the contents of those documents are true or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I'm sure that someone has interpreted them as accurately as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you cannot interpret those documents yourself, can you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish I could have spoken Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbian, but I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
